questions.q: If $|z-3+2 i| \leq 4$ then the difference between the greatest value and the least value of $|z|$ is
questions.solution:
$|z-(3-2 i)| \leq 4$ represents a circle whose centre is $(3,-2)$ and radius $=4$. $|z|=|z-0|$ represents the distance of point ' $z$ ' from origin $(0,0)$
Suppose $R S$ is the normal of the circle passing through origin ' $O$ ' and $G$ is its center $(3,-2)$ Here, $O R$ is the least distance and $O S$ is the greatest distance $O R=R G-O G and O S=O G+G S \ldots(1)$ As, $R G=G S=4O G=\sqrt{3^2+(-2)^2}=\sqrt{9+4}=\sqrt{13}$ From (1), $O R=4-\sqrt{13} and O S=4+\sqrt{13}$ So, required difference $\begin{aligned}$&=(4+$\sqrt{13})-($4-$\sqrt{13})$\\ &=$\sqrt{13}+\sqrt{13}=$2 $\sqrt{13} \end{aligned}$

questions.q: The set of all $\alpha \in R$, for which $w=\frac{1+(1-8 \alpha) z}{1-z}$ is a purely imaginary number, for all $z \in C$ satisfying $|z|=1$ and $\operatorname{Re} z \neq 1$, is
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}$&\because|z|=1 $\text{ \& } \operatorname{Re}$z  ≠ 1 \\
&$\text{ Suppose }$z=x+i y \Rightarrow x²+y²=1 \ldots \ldots($\mathrm{i})$\\
&$\text{ Now, }$w=$\frac{1+(1-8 \alpha) z}{1-z}$\\
&\Rightarrow w=$\frac{1+(1-8 \alpha)(x+i y)}{1-(x+i y)}$\\
&\Rightarrow w=$\frac{1+(1-8 \alpha)(x+i y))((1-\mathrm{x})+\mathrm{iy})}{1-(x+i y))((1-\mathrm{x})+\mathrm{iy})}$\\
&\Rightarrow \quad w=$\frac{\left[\left(1+x(1-8 \alpha)(1-x)-(1-8) y^2\right]\right.}{(1-x)^2+y^2}$\\
&+i $\frac{[(1+x(1-8 \alpha)) y-(1-8 \alpha) y(1-x)]}{(1-x)^2+y^2}
\end{aligned}$If, $w$ is purely imaginary. So,

$\begin{aligned}$&\operatorname{Re} w=$\frac{\left[(1+x(1-8 \alpha))(1-\alpha)-(1-8 \alpha) y^2\right]}{(1-x)^2+y^2}$\\
&=0 \\
&\Rightarrow(1-x)+x(1-8 $\alpha)($1-x)=(1-8) y² \\
&\Rightarrow(1-x)+x(1-8 $\alpha)-$x^2(1-8 $\alpha)=($1-8 x) y² \\
&\Rightarrow(1-x)+x(1-8 $\alpha)=$1-8 $\alpha$\\
&{$\left[\text{$ From }(i), x²+y²=1\right]}
\end{aligned}$\Rightarrow 1-8 \alpha=1\Rightarrow \alpha=0\therefore \alpha \in\{0\}$

Let $\omega$ be a complex number such that $2\omega + 1 = z$ where $z = \sqrt{- 3}$ . If

$\left|\begin{cases}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & - {\omega}^{2} - 1 & {\omega}^{2} \\ 1 & {\omega}^{2} & {\omega}^{7}\end{cases}\right| = 3k,$

questions.solution:
$\omega = - \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i$ (cube root of unity)

questions.q: Let $z = 1 + ai$, be a complex number, $a > 0$, such that ${z}^{3}$ is a real number. Then, the sum $1 + z + {z}^{2} + \ldots . + {z}^{11}$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
$z = 1 + ai$
Cubing both sides,
${z}^{3} = \left(1 - {a}^{2}\right) + 2ai + \left(1 - {a}^{2}\right)ai - 2{a}^{2}$
${z}^{3} = 1 - 3{a}^{2} + ( 3a - {a}^{3} ) i$
$∵ {z}^{3}$ is a real number.
$a\left(3 - {a}^{2}\right) = 0 ⇒ a = \sqrt{3} \left(a > 0\right)$

$1 + z + {z}^{2} \ldots . . {z}^{11} = \dfrac{{z}^{12} - 1}{z - 1} = \dfrac{{\left(1 + \sqrt{3}i\right)}^{12} - 1}{1 + \sqrt{3}i - 1} = \dfrac{{\left(1 + \sqrt{3}i\right)}^{12} - 1}{\sqrt{3}i}$

${\left(1 + \sqrt{3}i\right)}^{12} = {2}^{12}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i\right)}^{12} = {2}^{12}{\left(cos ⁡ \dfrac{\pi}{3} + isin ⁡ \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)}^{12} = {2}^{12}\left(cos ⁡ 4\pi + isin ⁡ 4\pi\right) = {2}^{12}$

$= \dfrac{{2}^{12} - 1}{\sqrt{3}i} = - 1365\sqrt{3}i$

questions.q: The point represented by $2 + i$ in the Argand plane moves $1$ unit eastwards, then $2$ units northwards and finally from there $2\sqrt{2}$ units in the south-west wards direction. Then its new position in the Argand plane is at the point represented by :

Let $P\left(2 + i\right) \text{ and } S(z)$
By Rotation theorem, rotating about $3 + 3i$, we get

$⇒ \dfrac{z - 3 - 3i}{- 2i} = 1 - i$

$⇒ z - 3 - 3i = - 2i - 2 ⇒ z = 1 + i$

questions.solution:
Let, $z = \dfrac{2 + 3isin\theta}{1 - 2isin\theta}$

Multiplying the denominator by its conjugate, we get,

$z = \dfrac{\left(2 + 3isin\theta\right)\left(1 + 2isin\theta\right)}{1 + 4\sin^{2}\theta}$

$= \dfrac{\left(2 - 6\sin^{2}\theta\right) + i\left(7sin\theta\right)}{1 + 4\sin^{2}\theta}$

To make it purely imaginary. Its real part should be $0$.

Hence, $2 = 6\sin^{2} ⁡ \theta$

$⇒ sin ⁡ \theta = \pm \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

questions.q: If $z$ is a non-real complex number, then the minimum value of $\dfrac{Im{z}^{5}}{{\left(Imz\right)}^{5}}$ is (Where $Imz =$ Imaginary part of $z$)
questions.solution:
Let, $z = r ( \text\cos\theta + i\text\sin\theta )$

${z}^{5} = {r}^{5} ( \text\cos5\theta + i\text\sin5\theta )$

$Im\left({z}^{5}\right) = {r}^{5}sin5\theta$

and ${\left(Imz\right)}^{5} = {r}^{5}\sin^{5}\theta$

$\dfrac{Im ( {z}^{5} )}{{\left(Imz\right)}^{5}} = \dfrac{sin5\theta}{\sin^{5}\theta} = A$(Let)

$⇒ \dfrac{dA}{d\theta} = \dfrac{5\sin^{5}\thetacos5\theta - 5sin5\theta\sin^{4}\thetacos\theta}{{\left(\sin^{5}\theta\right)}^{2}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dA}{d\theta} = \dfrac{5\sin^{4}\theta\left(sin\thetacos5\theta - sin5\thetacos\theta\right)}{\sin^{10}\theta}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dA}{d\theta} = \dfrac{5}{\sin^{6} \theta} \left[sin\left(- 4\theta\right)\right] = 0$

$⇒ \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$

The minimum value of $A$ will be at $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4} .$

$⇒ A = \dfrac{sin5\dfrac{\pi}{4}}{{\left(sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)}^{5}}$
$= \dfrac{\dfrac{- 1}{\sqrt{2}}}{{\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)}^{5}}$

$= - {\left(\sqrt{2}\right)}^{4} = - 4$

questions.q: If $2 + 3i$ is one of the roots of the equation $2{x}^{3} - 9{x}^{2} + kx - 13 = 0, k \in R,$ then the real root of this equation (where ${i}^{2} = - 1$) :
questions.solution:
If $2 + 3i$ in one of the roots, then $2 - 3i$ would be other.
Since coefficients of the equation are real.

Let $\gamma$ be the third root, then product of roots $\to \alpha\beta\gamma = \dfrac{13}{2}$
$\left(2 + 3i\right)\left(2 - 3i\right) ⋅ \gamma = \dfrac{13}{2}$
$\left(4 + 9\right) ⋅ \gamma = \dfrac{13}{2}$
$⇒ \gamma = \dfrac{1}{2}$

The value of k will come if we put $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$ in the equation
$2 ⋅ \dfrac{1}{8} - \dfrac{9}{4} + k ⋅ \dfrac{1}{2} - 13 = 0$
$⇒ \dfrac{k}{2} = 15$
$⇒ k = 30$
$∴$ Equation will become $2{x}^{3} - 9{x}^{2} + 30x - 13 = 0$
$⇒ \alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \gamma\alpha = \dfrac{30}{2} = 15$
$⇒ \left(2 + 3i\right)\dfrac{1}{2} + \left(2 - 3i\right)\dfrac{1}{2} + \left(2 + 3i\right)\left(2 - 3i\right) = 15$
$⇒ 1 + \dfrac{i}{2} + 1 - \dfrac{i}{2} + 13 = 15$
$⇒ 15 = 15$
Hence roots exists and is equal to $\dfrac{1}{2}$ '

questions.q: A complex number $z$ is said to be unimodular if $\left|z\right| = 1$. Let ${z}_{1} and {z}_{2}$ are complex numbers such that $\dfrac{{z}_{1} - 2{z}_{2}}{2 - {z}_{1}{z}_{2}}$ is unimodular and ${z}_{2}$ is not unimodular, then the point ${z}_{1}$ lies on a
questions.solution:
Given, $\dfrac{{z}_{1} - 2{z}_{2}}{2 - {z}_{1}\overset{¯}{z}2}$ is unimodular.

$⇒ \left|\dfrac{{z}_{1} - 2{z}_{2}}{2 - {z}_{1}\overset{¯}{z}2}\right| = 1$

$⇒ \left|{z}_{1} - 2{z}_{2}\right| = \left|2 - {z}_{1}\overset{¯}{z}2\right|$

Squaring both the sides, we get,

${\left|{z}_{1} - {2z}_{2}\right|}^{2} = {\left|2 - {z}_{1}{z}_{2}\right|}^{2}$

$⇒ \left({z}_{1} - 2{z}_{2}\right)\left(\overset{¯}{z}1 - 2\overset{¯}{z}2\right) = \left(2 - {z}_{1}\overset{¯}{z}2\right)\left(2 - \overset{¯}{z}1{z}_{2}\right)$

$\left(∵ {\left|z\right|}^{2} = z\overset{¯}{z}\right)$

$⇒ {z}_{1}\overset{¯}{z}1 - 2{z}_{1}\overset{¯}{z}2 - 2\overset{¯}{z}1{z}_{2} + 4\overset{¯}{z}2\overset{¯}{z}2$

$= 4 - 2\overset{¯}{z}1{z}_{2} - 2{z}_{1}\overset{¯}{z}2 + {z}_{1}\overset{¯}{z}1{z}_{2}\overset{¯}{z}2$

$⇒ {\left|{z}_{1}\right|}^{2} + 4{\left|{z}_{2}\right|}^{2} = 4 + {\left|{z}_{1}\right|}^{2}{\left|{z}_{2}\right|}^{2}$

$⇒ {\left|{z}_{1}\right|}^{2} - 4 + 4{\left|{z}_{2}\right|}^{2} - {\left|{z}_{1}\right|}^{2}{\left|{z}_{2}\right|}^{2} = 0$

$⇒ \left({\left|{z}_{1}\right|}^{2} - 4\right)\left(1 - {\left|{z}_{2}\right|}^{2}\right) = 0$

$⇒ \left|{z}_{1}\right| = 2$ or $\left|{z}_{2}\right| = 1$

Given, ${z}_{2}$ is not unimodular

$∴ \left|{z}_{1}\right| = 2$

$∴$ Point ${z}_{1}$ lies on a circle of radius $2$.

questions.q: If a complex number $z$ statisfies the equation $x+\sqrt{2}|z+1|+i=0$, then $|z|$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
Given equation is

$\begin{aligned}$& z+$\sqrt{2}|$z+1|+i=0 \\
& $\text{ put }$z=x+i y $\text{$ in the given equation. }\\
& (x+i y)+$\sqrt{2}|$x+i y+1|+i=0 \\
& \Rightarrow x+i y+$\sqrt{2}\left[\sqrt{(x+1)^2+y^2}\right]+$i=0
\end{aligned}

Now, equating real$ and imaginary part, we get\begin{aligned}$& x+$\sqrt{2} \sqrt{(x+1)^2+y^2}=$0 $\text{$ and }\\
& y+1=0 \Rightarrow y=-1 \\
& \Rightarrow x+$\sqrt{2} \sqrt{(x+1)^2+(-1)^2}=$0 \\
& \Rightarrow $\sqrt{2} \sqrt{(x+1)^2+1}=-$x \\
& \Rightarrow 2$\left[($x+1)^2+1\right]=x² \\
& \Rightarrow x²+4 x+4=0 \\
& \Rightarrow x=-2
\end{aligned}

Thus, $z=-2+i(-1) \Rightarrow|z|=\sqrt{5}$

options:

Let $z=x+$ iy $(\because x \neq 1$ as $z \neq 1)$z^2=\left(x^2-y^2\right)+i(2 x y)$\frac{z^2}{z-1}$ is real 
$\Rightarrow$ its imaginary part $=0$\Rightarrow 2 x y(x-1)-y\left(x^2-y^2\right)=0$\Rightarrow y\left(x^2+y^2-2 x\right)=0$\Rightarrow y=0 ; x^2+y^2-2 x=0$\therefore \mathrm{z}$ lies either on real axis or on a circle through origin.
